records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִד֙ אֶל־לִבּ֔וֹ עַתָּ֛ה אֶסָּפֶ֥ה יוֹם־אֶחָ֖ד בְּיַד־שָׁא֑וּל אֵֽין־לִ֨י ט֜וֹב כִּ֣י הִמָּלֵ֥ט אִמָּלֵ֣ט׀אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּ֗ים וְנוֹאַ֨שׁ מִמֶּ֤נִּי שָׁאוּל֙ לְבַקְשֵׁ֤נִי עוֹד֙ בְּכָל־גְּב֣וּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְנִמְלַטְתִּ֖י מִיָּדֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And said David to his heart, Now I will be swept away one day by [the] hand of Saul. There is nothing for me good but that I surely escape to [the] land of [the] Philistines, and will despair of me Saul, of seeking me again in all [the] territory of Israel, and I will escape from his hand.
pieces: But David said to himself, "One of these days Saul will destroy me. The best thing for me is to escape quickly to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will give up searching for me anywhere in Israel's territory, and I will be out of his reach."

L.1: And David said to his heart, "Now I will be swept away one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should surely escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will despair of seeking me any longer in all the territory of Israel, and I will escape from his hand."

R.1: But David thought to himself, "Someday Saul is going to kill me. The best thing I can do is to get away to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will stop looking for me all over Israel, and I will be safe from him."

decisions.choice: said to his heart: thought to himself
decisions.reason: To speak "to one's heart" is to say something inwardly, to think it over (Genesis 27:41). David is reasoning with himself; no one else hears him.

decisions.choice: swept away one day: destroyed some day
decisions.reason: The verb means to be swept away or brought to an end (12:25; 26:10). "One day" means at some time not yet known. Although Saul has just promised to do him no more harm (26:21, 25), David does not trust him.

decisions.choice: surely escape: escape without delay
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for emphasis. David sees escape as his only safe course and means to do it at once and in earnest.

decisions.choice: despair of: give up hope of
decisions.reason: The verb means to lose hope and give up (Ecclesiastes 2:20). Once David is outside Israel's borders, Saul will see no point in hunting for him there.

decisions.choice: said to himself (Balanced); thought to himself (Readable); out of his reach / safe from him
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the idioms of the heart and the hand into plain words. The hand stands for Saul's power to harm David, so "by the hand of Saul" becomes Saul as the one who acts.

records.heading: David among the Philistines

records.source: וַיָּ֣קָם דָּוִ֔ד וַיַּעֲבֹ֣ר ה֔וּא וְשֵׁשׁ־מֵא֥וֹת אִ֖ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עִמּ֑וֹ אֶל־אָכִ֥ישׁ בֶּן־מָע֖וֹךְ מֶ֥לֶךְ גַּֽת׃
records.gloss: And arose David and passed over, he and six hundred men who [were] with him, to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
pieces: So David set out and went over with the six hundred men who were with him to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.

L.2: And David arose and passed over, he and the six hundred men who [were] with him, to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.

R.2: So David and his six hundred men left and went over to Achish, the son of Maoch. Achish was the king of the Philistine city of Gath.

decisions.choice: Achish king of Gath: the king David fled to before
decisions.reason: David had gone to Achish once before, alone, and escaped only by pretending to be mad (21:11-16). Now he comes with an armed band and offers his service. Gath was one of the five chief Philistine cities (6:17) and Goliath's home (17:4).

decisions.choice: passed over: crossed over to the other side
decisions.reason: The verb means to cross over. David goes over from Israel to its enemy, a step that changes his standing in the story (29:3-4).

decisions.choice: six hundred men: David's band, grown from four hundred
decisions.reason: David first gathered about four hundred men (22:2); by 23:13 they numbered about six hundred. A band this size, with their families (verse 3), was a small fighting force.

decisions.choice: the Philistine city of Gath
decisions.reason: Readable reminds the reader that Gath was a Philistine city, as in 21:11, and gives the king's title its own sentence.

records.source: וַיֵּשֶׁב֩ דָּוִ֨ד עִם־אָכִ֥ישׁ בְּגַ֛ת ה֥וּא וַאֲנָשָׁ֖יו אִ֣ישׁ וּבֵית֑וֹ דָּוִד֙ וּשְׁתֵּ֣י נָשָׁ֔יו אֲחִינֹ֨עַם֙ הַיִּזְרְעֵאלִ֔ית וַאֲבִיגַ֥יִל אֵֽשֶׁת־נָבָ֖ל הַֽכַּרְמְלִֽית׃
records.gloss: And dwelt David with Achish in Gath, he and his men, each and his household, David and two his wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelite and Abigail [the] wife of Nabal, the Carmelite.
pieces: David and his men settled with Achish in Gath, each man with his household. David had his two wives with him, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail of Carmel, Nabal's widow.

L.3: And David dwelt with Achish in Gath, he and his men, each [with] his household, David and his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelite and Abigail the wife of Nabal, the Carmelite.

R.3: David and his men lived in Gath with Achish, and each man had his family with him. David's two wives were with him too. They were Ahinoam from the town of Jezreel and Abigail from Carmel, who had been Nabal's wife.

decisions.choice: each with his household: whole families moved
decisions.reason: The men brought their wives and children with them (30:3). David's band was settling in Philistine land, not making a short raid.

decisions.choice: Ahinoam and Abigail: the wives David married in chapter 25
decisions.reason: David married Abigail after Nabal's death and also took Ahinoam of Jezreel (25:39-43). Jezreel here is probably the town in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:56), not the better-known Jezreel in the north.

decisions.choice: the Carmelite: the woman from Carmel, that is, Abigail
decisions.reason: The word "Carmelite" has a feminine form, so it describes Abigail, not Nabal. Carmel was the town in Judah where Nabal kept his flocks (25:2). "Wife of Nabal" names her by her late husband, so she is his widow (25:39).

decisions.choice: of Carmel, Nabal's widow (Balanced); from Carmel, who had been Nabal's wife (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "the wife of Nabal". Since Nabal had died, Balanced says "widow" and Readable says she "had been" his wife. Both attach "Carmel" to Abigail, as the Hebrew does.

records.source: וַיֻּגַּ֣ד לְשָׁא֔וּל כִּֽי־בָרַ֥ח דָּוִ֖ד גַּ֑ת וְלֹֽא־יָסַ֥ף ע֖וֹד לְבַקְשֽׁוֹ׃ס
records.gloss: And it was told to Saul that had fled David [to] Gath, and not he again continued to seek him.
pieces: When word reached Saul that David had fled to Gath, he stopped searching for him.

L.4: And it was told to Saul that David had fled [to] Gath, and he did not again seek him any longer.

R.4: Someone told Saul that David had run away to Gath. So Saul stopped looking for him.

decisions.choice: no longer sought him: David's reasoning proves right
decisions.reason: What David expected in verse 1 comes about: once David is outside Israel, Saul stops hunting him. The words echo verse 1 ("seeking me any longer").

decisions.choice: he continued: the reading noted in the margin
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text spell the verb in a slightly different form, and the reading noted by the scribes in the margin gives the usual form. The meaning is the same either way.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר דָּוִ֜ד אֶל־אָכִ֗ישׁ אִם־נָא֩ מָצָ֨אתִי חֵ֤ן בְּעֵינֶ֨יךָ֙ יִתְּנוּ־לִ֣י מָק֗וֹם בְּאַחַ֛ת עָרֵ֥י הַשָּׂדֶ֖ה וְאֵ֣שְׁבָה שָּׁ֑ם וְלָ֨מָּה יֵשֵׁ֧ב עַבְדְּךָ֛ בְּעִ֥יר הַמַּמְלָכָ֖ה עִמָּֽךְ׃
records.gloss: And said David to Achish, If please I have found favor in your eyes, let them give to me a place in one [of the] towns of the field, and I will dwell there. And why should dwell your servant in [the] city of the kingdom with you?
pieces: Then David said to Achish, "If I have found favor with you, please let me be given a place in one of the country towns, so that I can live there. Why should your servant live in the royal city with you?"

L.5: And David said to Achish, "If, please, I have found favor in your eyes, let them give me a place in one of the towns of the countryside, and I will dwell there. For why should your servant dwell in the royal city with you?"

R.5: Then David said to Achish, "If you are pleased with me, please give me a place in one of the towns out in the country. I can live there. There is no need for me to live with you in the king's city."

decisions.choice: found favor in your eyes: if you are pleased with me
decisions.reason: A polite way of asking a favor of someone of higher rank (20:29; Genesis 18:3).

decisions.choice: towns of the field: country towns
decisions.reason: "The field" is the open country, away from the capital. David asks for a town of his own at a distance from Gath.

decisions.choice: your servant ... the royal city: a humble request with a hidden purpose
decisions.reason: David speaks of himself as "your servant", a polite way of saying "me", and makes it sound as if he is too lowly to live in the king's city. Away from Achish's eyes he will be free to act as he pleases, as verses 8-12 show.

decisions.choice: There is no need for me to live with you in the king's city.
decisions.reason: Readable turns David's question into the statement it implies and says "me" for the polite "your servant".

records.source: וַיִּתֶּן־ל֥וֹ אָכִ֛ישׁ בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא אֶת־צִֽקְלָ֑ג לָכֵ֞ן הָיְתָ֤ה צִֽקְלַג֙ לְמַלְכֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And gave to him Achish on the day the that Ziklag; therefore has belonged Ziklag to [the] kings of Judah until the day the this.
pieces: So that day Achish gave him Ziklag. That is why Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.

L.6: And Achish gave him Ziklag on that day; therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.

R.6: So that day Achish gave David the town of Ziklag. That is why Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.

decisions.choice: Ziklag: a town in the far south
decisions.reason: Ziklag lay in the south of the land, toward the Negev. It had been listed among the towns of Judah and of Simeon (Joshua 15:31; 19:5), but it was then in Philistine hands. From here David could raid the desert peoples to the south (verse 8).

decisions.choice: to this day: up to the writer's own time
decisions.reason: As in 5:5, the phrase refers to the time when the book was written. "The kings of Judah" suggests a writer who knew the line of David's descendants who reigned in Judah, long after these events.

decisions.choice: the town of Ziklag
decisions.reason: Readable adds "the town of" so that the unfamiliar name is clear, and names David for "him".

records.source: וַֽיְהִי֙ מִסְפַּ֣ר הַיָּמִ֔ים אֲשֶׁר־יָשַׁ֥ב דָּוִ֖ד בִּשְׂדֵ֣ה פְלִשְׁתִּ֑ים יָמִ֖ים וְאַרְבָּעָ֥ה חֳדָשִֽׁים׃
records.gloss: And was the number of the days which dwelt David in [the] field of [the] Philistines days and four months.
pieces: David lived in Philistine territory for a year and four months.

L.7: And the number of the days that David dwelt in the country of the Philistines was days and four months.

R.7: David lived in the land of the Philistines for a year and four months.

decisions.choice: days: a year
decisions.reason: "Days" can stand for a full year, as in 1:3 and 2:19, where "from days to days" means every year, and Judges 17:10. So the time is a year and four months. The early Greek translation has only "four months".

decisions.choice: the field of the Philistines: the Philistines' country
decisions.reason: "Field" here means territory or region (also verse 11).

decisions.choice: a year and four months
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "days"; Balanced and Readable give the sense explained in the meaning decision.

records.heading: David raids from Ziklag

records.source: וַיַּ֤עַל דָּוִד֙ וַֽאֲנָשָׁ֔יו וַֽיִּפְשְׁט֛וּ אֶל־הַגְּשׁוּרִ֥י וְהַגִּזְרִ֖י וְהָעֲמָלֵקִ֑י כִּ֣י הֵ֜נָּה יֹשְׁב֤וֹת הָאָ֨רֶץ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר מֵֽעוֹלָ֔ם בּוֹאֲךָ֥ שׁ֖וּרָה וְעַד־אֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: And went up David and his men and they raided against the Geshurite[s] and the Gizrite[s] and the Amalekite[s], for they [were] dwelling [in] the land which [was] from of old, your coming toward Shur and as far as [the] land of Egypt.
pieces: David and his men would go up and raid the Geshurites, the Gizrites and the Amalekites. These peoples had lived in the land from ancient times, in the region that stretches toward Shur and on to the land of Egypt.

L.8: And David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites and the Gizrites and the Amalekites, for they [were] the inhabitants of the land from of old, as you go toward Shur and as far as the land of Egypt.

R.8: David and his men would go out and attack the Geshurites, the Gizrites and the Amalekites. These peoples had lived for a very long time in the land that reaches toward the desert of Shur and as far as Egypt.

decisions.choice: Geshurites, Gizrites, Amalekites: desert peoples of the south
decisions.reason: These were peoples living in the dry south between Philistia and Egypt. These Geshurites are the southern ones of Joshua 13:2, not the Geshur north-east of Galilee. The Amalekites were Israel's old enemies (Exodus 17:8-16; 15:2-3).

decisions.choice: the Gizrites: the reading noted in the margin
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text spell the name "Girzites", and the reading noted by the scribes in the margin has "Gizrites", which may mean people linked with the town of Gezer. The name is known only here, so it is uncertain which form is original.

decisions.choice: from of old: the land they had lived in for ages
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "from of old" says these peoples had long lived there. Some copies of the early Greek translation read a place name, "from Telam" (compare Telaim in 15:4). The Hebrew text is followed here.

decisions.choice: toward Shur, as far as Egypt: the same region as 15:7
decisions.reason: Shur was the desert east of Egypt (Genesis 16:7; Exodus 15:22). Saul struck the Amalekites "from Havilah toward Shur, which is east of Egypt" (15:7), yet Amalekites still live there, and they return in chapter 30.

decisions.choice: went up and raided: the first of many raids
decisions.reason: Verses 8-11 describe what David did again and again during his time at Ziklag; verse 11 says this was "his practice". This verse tells the raids as one story, and the next verses use forms for repeated action.

decisions.choice: would go up and raid
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "would" to show that these raids happened many times, as verses 9-11 make plain.

records.source: וְהִכָּ֤ה דָוִד֙ אֶת־הָאָ֔רֶץ וְלֹ֥א יְחַיֶּ֖ה אִ֣ישׁ וְאִשָּׁ֑ה וְלָקַח֩ צֹ֨אן וּבָקָ֜ר וַחֲמֹרִ֤ים וּגְמַלִּים֙ וּבְגָדִ֔ים וַיָּ֖שָׁב וַיָּבֹ֥א אֶל־אָכִֽישׁ׃
records.gloss: And would strike David the land, and not he would let live man and woman, and he would take sheep and cattle and donkeys and camels and clothes, and he returned and came to Achish.
pieces: Whenever David attacked the region, he left no man or woman alive. He took the sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels and clothing, and then came back to Achish.

L.9: And David would strike the land and would not let man or woman live, and he would take sheep and cattle and donkeys and camels and clothing, and he returned and came to Achish.

R.9: Each time David attacked an area, he killed every man and woman. He took their sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels and clothes. Then he went back to Achish.

decisions.choice: would strike ... would not let live ... would take: repeated action
decisions.reason: The verbs are in a form that describes what happened again and again, so this is what David did on every raid, not on one occasion.

decisions.choice: not letting man or woman live: so that no one could report
decisions.reason: Verse 11 gives the reason: no survivor must reach Gath to tell what David was really doing. The story reports this plainly; it does not say God commanded it.

decisions.choice: sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, clothing: the plunder
decisions.reason: These were the wealth of desert herding peoples. David brings the plunder back, and Achish presumably receives a share as his overlord (compare 30:26).

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אָכִ֔ישׁ אַל־פְּשַׁטְתֶּ֖ם הַיּ֑וֹם וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֗ד עַל־נֶ֤גֶב יְהוּדָה֙ וְעַל־נֶ֣גֶב הַיַּרְחְמְאֵלִ֔י וְאֶל־נֶ֖גֶב הַקֵּינִֽי׃
records.gloss: And would say Achish, Not have you raided the day? And would say David, Against [the] Negev of Judah, and against [the] Negev of the Jerahmeelite[s], and against [the] Negev of the Kenite[s].
pieces: When Achish asked, "Did you not go raiding today?" David would answer, "Against the Negev of Judah," or "Against the Negev of the Jerahmeelites," or "Against the Negev of the Kenites."

L.10: And Achish would say, "Have you not raided today?" And David would say, "Against the Negev of Judah," or "Against the Negev of the Jerahmeelites," or "Against the Negev of the Kenites."

R.10: Achish would ask him, "You went raiding today, did you not?" David would answer, "Yes, against the southern part of Judah." Or he would say, "Against the south, where the Jerahmeelites live," or "Against the south, where the Kenites live."

decisions.choice: Have you not raided today?: the Hebrew as it stands
alternatives: Against whom did you raid today?
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has the word for "not", making a question that expects the answer "yes". The early Greek translation reads "Against whom did you raid today?", which fits David's answers well and may reflect a slightly different Hebrew word. The Hebrew text is followed here.

decisions.choice: Judah, the Jerahmeelites, the Kenites: David's own people and their friends
decisions.reason: The Negev is the dry south. The Jerahmeelites were a clan of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:9, 25), and the Kenites were friends of Israel who lived among Judah (15:6; Judges 1:16). David names Israel's own south to make Achish believe he is attacking his own people (verse 12). In truth he raided Israel's enemies (verse 8).

decisions.choice: would say: a repeated exchange
decisions.reason: Like verse 9, this describes what happened after each raid. David gave one of these answers each time.

decisions.choice: Yes; the southern part of Judah; where the Jerahmeelites live
decisions.reason: Readable adds "Yes" to show that Achish's question expects it, and explains "Negev" as the south and the clan names as the people living there.

records.source: וְאִ֨ישׁ וְאִשָּׁ֜ה לֹֽא־יְחַיֶּ֣ה דָוִ֗ד לְהָבִ֥יא גַת֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר פֶּן־יַגִּ֥דוּ עָלֵ֖ינוּ לֵאמֹ֑ר כֹּֽה־עָשָׂ֤ה דָוִד֙ וְכֹ֣ה מִשְׁפָּט֔וֹ כָּל־הַ֨יָּמִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָשַׁ֖ב בִּשְׂדֵ֥ה פְלִשְׁתִּֽים׃
records.gloss: And man and woman not would let live David to bring [to] Gath, saying, Lest they tell about us, saying, Thus has done David. And thus [was] his practice all the days which he dwelt in [the] field of [the] Philistines.
pieces: David left no man or woman alive to bring to Gath, for he thought, "They might report on us and say, 'This is what David did.'" This was his practice the whole time he lived in Philistine territory.

L.11: And David would not let man or woman live to bring [them to] Gath, saying, "Lest they tell about us, saying, 'Thus David has done.'" And thus [was] his practice all the days that he dwelt in the country of the Philistines.

R.11: David did not leave any man or woman alive to be brought back to Gath. He thought, "They might tell what we did. They would say, 'This is what David has been doing.'" David did this the whole time he lived in the land of the Philistines.

decisions.choice: saying: David's reason, in his own thoughts
decisions.reason: "Saying" here introduces what David had in mind, his reason for leaving no survivors, not words spoken aloud.

decisions.choice: and such was his practice: the narrator's words
alternatives: part of what the survivors would report
decisions.reason: The last clause could still belong to what the survivors might report ("this is what David did, and this was his way the whole time"). It is read here as the narrator's own summary, closing the account of the raids that began in verse 8.

decisions.choice: his practice: his custom, his way of doing things
decisions.reason: The word usually means a ruling or judgment, but it can also mean a custom or usual way (2:13; 8:9). Here it is David's regular way of acting.

decisions.choice: he thought ... They might report on us
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable express "lest" as "might" and make clear that this was David's thinking.

records.source: וַיַּאֲמֵ֥ן אָכִ֖ישׁ בְּדָוִ֣ד לֵאמֹ֑ר הַבְאֵ֤שׁ הִבְאִישׁ֙ בְּעַמּ֣וֹ בְיִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְהָ֥יָה לִ֖י לְעֶ֥בֶד עוֹלָֽם׃פ
records.gloss: And trusted Achish in David, saying, He has surely made himself stink among his people, in Israel, and he will be to me [a] slave forever.
pieces: Achish trusted David and thought, "He has made himself utterly hated by his own people, the Israelites, so he will be my servant for life."

L.12: And Achish trusted David, saying, "He has surely made himself a stench among his people, in Israel, and he will be my slave forever."

R.12: Achish believed David. He thought, "David has made his own people, the Israelites, hate him completely. So he will have to serve me for the rest of his life."

decisions.choice: made himself a stench: made himself hated
decisions.reason: The verb means to stink. To make oneself a stench to someone is to make them loathe you (13:4; 2 Samuel 10:6). The verb is doubled for emphasis: Achish thinks David's own people now utterly loathe him.

decisions.choice: a slave forever: bound to serve for life
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of a slave who stays with his master for life (Deuteronomy 15:17; Exodus 21:6). Achish thinks David can never go home, so he must be loyal to Achish for good. David is in fact deceiving him, and the reader sees the irony (29:6-9).

decisions.choice: saying: what Achish thought
decisions.reason: As in verse 11, "saying" introduces a person's thoughts. Achish does not say this to David.

decisions.choice: servant (Balanced); serve me (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "slave"; Balanced and Readable say "servant" and "serve", following the usual rule for this word. The meaning decision keeps the sense of lifelong bondage.
